Title: GM boosts supplier relations and EV supply chain resilience | Automotive Logistics
Raw_Content_Text: ![Go to frontpage. Logo, Automotive Logistics](/view-resources/ultima/public/al/logo.svg) # GM’s strategy to tackle EV logistics challenges: Digitalisation, nearshoring, and improving supplier relations ## Strengthening supplier relationships, nearshoring strategies and digitalisation are enabling GM to enhance supply chain resilience across North America. From securing critical EV components to optimising cross-border logistics, the carmaker is fostering innovation and operational efficiency amid growing challenges. Strengthening supplier relationships, nearshoring strategies and digitalisation are enabling GM to enhance supply chain resilience across North America. From securing critical EV components to optimising cross-border logistics, the carmaker is fostering innovation and operational efficiency amid growing challenges. ![Ultium Cells' Lansing site](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/177103.webp?imageId=177103&width=960&height=540&format=jpg "Ultium Cells’ Lansing siteUltium Cells is a joint venture between GM and LG Chem") The automotive supply chain has been in turmoil over recent years, and *Automotive Logistics’* recent analysis has shown that [OEMs are facing increasing cost pressures](https://www.automotivelogistics.media/supply-chain-management/automotive-logistics-providers-are-experiencing-increasing-cost-pressures/46474.article " Analysis: Automotive logistics providers are experiencing increasing cost pressures"). In response, GM has embarked on strengthening supplier relationships, embracing nearshoring strategies, and is leveraging digitalisation to tackle critical challenges. By fostering long-term partnerships, securing regional capacity and improving supply chain visibility, GM is building resilience in an increasingly complex market. #### Strengthening automotive supplier relations for supply chain resilience Strengthening supplier relations can improve resiliency, something that Covid and the semiconductor crisis taught automotive logistics firms. In GM’s case, the carmaker “flexed the muscle” of getting deeper into its value chain to understand where its raw materials are coming from and map out its key suppliers’ sub-tiers and where they are located. Prioritising strategic, long-term partnerships over more transactional ones, especially for critical logistics lanes and EV components, allowed GM to manage those n-tier suppliers better. The OEM now actively collaborates directly with its semiconductor and raw material suppliers to help ensure long-term stability. “If you were to compare and contrast other OEMs with GM, there is a definite difference in terms of how we manage [relationships]. One of the things that I ask for in return, because nothing is free, is preference,” said Jeff Morrison, vice-president of global purchasing and supply chain at GM, at [ALSC Global 2024](https://www.automotivelogistics.media/automotive-logistics-and-supply-chain-global "Automotive Logistics & Supply Chain Global 2024"). “As you’re allocating capacity out, please do not forget your anchor partners. Please give us the preference that I think we have earned over this amount of time, and I promise you, if you don’t give us that preference, we will probably not forget that either.” GM Mexico has been working closely with its local suppliers to foster innovation and secure critical components, all the while enhancing regional capacity. Mónica García, director of global procurement and supply chain at GM Mexico said the carmaker is further promoting these supplier relationships by providing training, digitalisation initiatives and joint problem-solving efforts to strengthen resilience. #### Tackling EV supply chain challenges with nearshoring and battery localisation Cost pressures across automotive logistics are escalating in a difficult market where EV supply and consumer demand remains unbalanced, and GM finds itself in the same boat. Morrison said that from an EV standpoint, the battery is the biggest cost driver through both material costs and logistics costs. To combat this, GM is using battery localisation, as well as gaining more visibility of its raw material suppliers. Morrison said the carmaker is working on building out the value chain going back to the raw material mines and manufacturing battery cells in the US with its partners. ![ALSC Mexico 2024 Red sofa Monica Garcia GM](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/177104.webp?imageId=177104&width=960&height=642&format=jpg "Mónica García, GM at ALSC Mexico 2024") Morrison highlighted priorities for GM’s logistics team, including profitability, network optimisation, and securing critical global flows, particularly in RoRo and cross-border freight. He warned of the risk of disruption without proactive collaboration. Similarly, GM is strategically leveraging nearshoring to reduce dependency on complex global supply chains. Cultivating regional supplier networks has allowed the company to improve its supply chain agility and mitigate risks. An example of this can be found in GM Mexico. Mónica García, director of global procurement and supply chain at GM Mexico said that nearshoring has brought the division benefits including reduced transport costs, shorter lead times, and improved inventory management. #### Optimising cross-border logistics and operational excellence GM has improved cross-border operations, expecially between the US and Mexico, by addressing capacity issues through stronger partnerships, operational focus, and reducing waste. Morrison stressed efficient container management, citing opportunities to reduce costs by improving utilisation of capacity. ![Jeff Morrison GM ALSC Global 2024](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/177105.webp?imageId=177105&width=960&height=696&format=jpg "Jeff Morrison, GM at ALSC Global 2024") The carmaker looked specifically at operational efficiency at the border, identifying and addressing the “blocking and tackling” challenges that can impede freight movements. Spotlighting target areas like this can free up bottlenecks and improve the flow of supply. However, when looking specifically at the US-Mexico border, there is heightened demand on the infrastructure due to increased nearshoring and competition from new entrants to the market. And, with the upcoming tariffs promised by president-elect Donald Trump, these cross-border logistics may prove more difficult – and expensive. While the market waits to see if the import tariffs will be implemented at the start of 2025, digitalisation may offer a solution to current bottlenecks. At GM, digitalisation efforts are focused on two key areas: improving transparency across the supply chain and increasing operational efficiency. By leveraging advanced data analytics and real-time monitoring systems, GM has been able to track supply chain performance, identify bottlenecks, and respond proactively to potential disruptions. This has been especially important in navigating challenges such as component shortages, volatile demand patterns and logistics delays, said García. While digitalisation offers significant advantages, García acknowledged that challenges remain, particularly for smaller suppliers that may lack the resources to implement sophisticated systems. However, she expressed optimism that continued collaboration and investment in technology will drive widespread adoption across Mexico’s automotive ecosystem. ## ## ## ## Events[View more](https://www.automotivelogistics.media/events) ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/2549714.webp?imageId=2549714&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&heightx=0.00&heighty=0.00&heightw=100.00&heighth=100.00&width=384&height=258&format=jpg "17-19 March 2026") ## 17-19 March 2026 ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/2549729.webp?imageId=2549729&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&heightx=0.00&heighty=0.00&heightw=100.00&heighth=100.00&width=384&height=258&format=jpg "21-23 April 2026") ## 21-23 April 2026 ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/2549737.webp?imageId=2549737&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=100.00&croph=100.00&heightx=0.00&heighty=0.00&heightw=100.00&heighth=100.00&width=384&height=258&format=jpg "9-10 June 2026") ## 9-10 June 2026 ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/2549741.webp?imageId=2549741&x=0.00&y=0.00&cropw=99.18&croph=100.00&heightx=0.00&heighty=0.00&heightw=100.00&heighth=100.00&width=384&height=258&format=jpg "27-28 October 2026") ## 27-28 October 2026 ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/2549745.webp?imageId=2549745&x=0.27&y=0.00&cropw=98.77&croph=100.00&heightx=0.00&heighty=0.00&heightw=100.00&heighth=100.00&width=384&height=258&format=jpg "10-12 November 2026") ## 10-12 November 2026 ![](https://image.automotivelogistics.media/105747.webp?imageId=105747&width=960&height=432&format=jpg) ## ## Automotive Logistics is the leading resource for automotive logistics and supply chain professionals globally. With Sphera’s *N*-Tier Transparency solution, Supply Chain and Procurement leaders can map upstream and midstream suppliers, uncovering hidden risks before they escalate into critical disruptions. ![image of two people looking at a computer screen](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Product-Hero-SCT-N-Tier.webp) Identify and mitigate vulnerabilities with a comprehensive view of supplier relationships and dependencies across your network. By reducing blind spots, improving data accuracy, and providing real-time risk insights, organizations can stay ahead of supplier and supply chain disruptions, compliance issues, and reputational threats. ## Beyond visibility: Gain *N*-Tier transparency Seeing your Tier 2–3 suppliers is just the beginning, true *N*-Tier transparency requires accurate, reliable data and a comprehensive view of supplier relationships. While many organizations believe they have visibility beyond Tier 1, gaps in data and insights leave them vulnerable to hidden risks across their supply networks. With Sphera’s holistic *N*-Tier solution, organizations can proactively address disruptions, regulatory compliance issues, and reputational threats, ensuring risk mitigation strategies are comprehensive. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Get Full Visibility of All Corporate and Operational Risks ](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Get-Full-Visibility-of-All-Corporate-and-Operational-Risks-.webp) ![](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Automated-invitation-process-copy.png) ## Enhancing Supplier Engagement The number of *N*-Tier solutions available to corporations to manage and improve the Tier 2-3 supplier visibility is growing exponentially. Unfortunately, managing them has become a resource-intensive balancing act involving unverified data and generic high-volume unmanageable lists and a lack of actionable intelligence. Sphera’s SCT *N*-Tier solution delivers: **Ease of Use** User-friendly interface and navigation to support clarity of information and intelligence in the mapping process **Weighted Supplier Selection** Maintain control of supplier selection in order to align *N*-Tier mapping and transparency with your wider supply chain strategy **Scalable** SCTs *N*-Tier solution is infinitely scalable and supports your supplier growth as well as your duo and multi-supplier strategy **Accurate Risk Monitoring** With 99.8% risk monitoring accuracy, gain access to multi-tier risk alerts and real-time monitoring across your supplier network and supply chain ## Stay in control With Sphera’s *N*-Tier solution, you remain in full control of your verification process, ensuring transparency aligns with your broader supply chain strategy. A user-friendly interface and intuitive navigation provide clear insights into supplier relationships, making the mapping process seamless and efficient. Maintain complete oversight of supplier selection, allowing you to proactively manage risks, enhance compliance, and strengthen supply chain resilience with confidence. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Verified Sub Tier Relations’](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Verified-Sub-Tier-Relations.webp) ## Benefits *N*-Tier Risk Intelligence Avoid disruptions caused by lower-tier suppliers with automated risk alerts providing you with the insight needed to respond proactively and with speed. Intelligent Sourcing Gain seamless intelligence into suppliers outside your supplier network to make intelligent decisions aligned with your duo– or multi–supplier sourcing strategy Compliance Simplify regulatory compliance by gaining access into multiple echelons within your entire supplier network. Verify your Tier 2 and 3 suppliers adhere to regulations. Visibility With full visibility into global supplier networks, you can quickly and successfully shift production between suppliers should issues arise deeper in the supply chain. ![Navigating supply chains in an ESG world end page](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Navigating-supply-chains-in-an-ESG-world-end-page.webp) ## Read the *N*-Tier eBook Read our eBook to see how top procurement and supply chain leaders handled major supplier crises. ## Read the *N*-Tier Survey Report Download our report to see how leaders approach N-Tier transparency, and spot gaps in your own supply chain. ![Download our report to see how leaders approach N-Tier transparency, and spot gaps in your own supply chain.](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/n-tier-report-min.jpg) ## Request a demo Fill out the form and we will get back to you to discuss your sub-tier visibility needs. ## Resources ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%201996%201496'%2F%3E) #### Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report 2026 ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%207721%205150'%2F%3E) #### AI-Powered Supplier Risk Management Survey 2025 ![aerial view of container ship](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%201422%20800'%2F%3E) #### Future-Proofing Supply Chains: AI as a Risk Management Game Changer ### Explore the modules in this suite Our enterprise-wide, fully integrated software reduces the likelihood of incidents and operational losses. Advanced software tools build workflows to capture, track, investigate, report and analyze health and safety information. Risk Radar Leverage the power of AI to map and proactively protect your supply network. Impact Analyzer Assess the criticality of suppliers and detect vulnerabilities. Experts........................................................................................................66-68 GLOBALCLEANTECH100 CONTENTS January 2025 3 That was in the middle of a period some labelled, with the benefit of hindsight, as cleantech 1.0 (albeit it was more accurately renewables 1.0, given the dominance of investments in that period of solar, wind, batteries and biofuels, and the lack of investment at that time in 80% of the cleantech problem-set). There are signals I see in this year’s Global Cleantech 100 – in the process (and the expert panellist’s comments), and in the outcomes (the companies) and in the analysis and insights contained herein - that we are in, or close to, some kind of change period on the barometer. Maybe in a few years 2024/2025 will retrospectively be referenced as the end of climatetech 2.0, and the start of a new phase? No doubt Trump 2.0 will be a factor in such, too. From the comments used (anonymously) by our expert panel on companies in the shortlist, the picture of a more sober and skeptical market emerges. On the one hand we have the negative-type commentary, the words that indicate what is top of mind for an increasing number of market players: n  Hype is called out in much more obvious prevalence this year, as illustrated in these comments. – “ Lots of hype for years but still haven’t scaled to even pilot and doesn’t have a commercial design.” – “ Years of hype and raises but haven’t seen any scale or relevant deployment that went past announcement.” – “ Dubious. A lot of hype, but it is brute force and very expensive.” – “ Full of news, but nothing works and nothing ships. I no longer believe the story.” n  These kind of comments speak to the underlying concern and a stronger scrutiny of the economics and scalability of anything and everything: – “ Likely never cost-effective.” – “ Really dubious the product pencils economically.” – “ Scalability of process is now under question; cost too high and efficiency gain too low.” FOREWORD WRITTEN BY RICHARD YOUNGMAN, CEO, CLEANTECH GROUP It has been 16 years since we first started the Global Cleantech 100 – in 2009 – to act as an annual barometer on global cleantech innovation. THERE ARE SIGNALS I SEE IN THIS YEAR’S GLOBAL CLEANTECH 100 THAT WE ARE IN, OR CLOSE TO, SOME KIND OF CHANGE PERIOD ON THE BAROMETER GLOBALCLEANTECH100 CONTENTS January 2025 4 On the other hand, we have clues as to what is required to gain widespread trust and support in today’s investment market: n  The importance of demonstrable progress towards commercialization, the ability to get there, and the ability to scale reliably once there, are all highly prized. These comments are illustrative thereof: – “ Their technology is a low cost solution and this is essential technology for mass penetration of renewable energy.” – “ Great team, impactful tech, commercial traction, need we say more…” – “ Crazy strong traction and growth, with no churn - and huge opportunity set in multiple large verticals.” n  And where something is unproven and pre-commercialization, the bar seems to have significantly been raised. The cost trajectory needs to have outstanding potential, and not be over-sold, to gain strong support: – “ Interesting and unique approach that would potentially reduce the cost dramatically.” – “ This means that the cost, footprint, complexity and speed of solution are all dramatically improved.” – “ A credible story lead by a credible CEO. They are not claiming cost parity next year, but rather putting forward realistic plans to get within spitting distance in the 2030’s. That is real.” – “ More CAPEX-intensive model, today, but big impact on lowering cost… – “ Novel process. Seems highly scalable and low-cost.” – “ Unique value proposition, as the market looks for low cost capabilities. Major OEMs involved.” In addition to these general sentiment observations, I would point to three trends I see in the identity of the 2025 Global Cleantech 100 companies themselves: 1.  There is a clear sense of a flight to traction and execution plays. Think companies such as: –  BasiGo, Crux, LevelTen Energy, Omnidian, PVcase, and Raptor Maps 2.  There are more solutions in this year’s 100 than ever before that relate to the earth’s hardcore (and its geology), on the one hand, and its oceans, on the other: –  CorPower Ocean and Ebb Carbon speak to the latter; 44.01, Fervo Energy, Heirloom, Koloma, and Vaulted Deep speak to the former 3.  Water innovation features more strongly than it has done for many years, as per the following companies –  Aclarity, Aqua Membranes, Indra, Moleaer, Pani, and ZwitterCo. Are we finally waking up to the water crisis coming our way in the 2030s? Exaggerated, unrealistic promises made in the hot markets of 2020-21 have come home to roost. It is especially felt in sectoral areas like hydrogen and carbon capture. Some of the old favorites and Global Cleantech 100 companies have not made the list, where they have not commanded a strong level of consensus support across the market this year. Some in the market have seen enough in recent years and need to see more from them to believe in their long-term story. As we look forward to 2025, market sentiments today suggests that we will see two obvious consequences: 1.  Less of the shiny new objects – and certainly ones that are fully reliant on U.S. federal policy and taxpayer support will struggle 2.  Less of the “me-too’s” – with capital more scarce, the best and the reasonably valued should flourish as there may be fewer, well-funded competitors. The market is still open to new technologies and approaches. It’s not as if some of the forerunners have obviously and fully got the future solution set tied up; the anaemic M&A/IPO environment, as described in the Graduates section, is testament to that. However, the bar has gone up for what kind of level of potential novelty, uniqueness, and cost improvements might be attractive. A more sober, skeptical environment and a return to fundamentals is apparent. RY FOREWORD As Climate Tech companies pioneer innovations for a sustainable future, they encounter distinct challenges stemming from the novel nature of their operations and the pressing need to scale quickly within a low-carbon economy. Significant investments from Venture Caps and Private Equity funds, coupled with Government incentives, has propelled the growth in Climate Tech. Raw_Content_Text: ![Sphera Logo](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo.png) ![Sphera Logo (White Version)](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![sphera logo](/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) # *N*-Tier Transparency Effective risk monitoring goes beyond Tier 1 suppliers, it extends across the entire *N*-Tier network. With Sphera’s *N*-Tier Transparency solution, Supply Chain and Procurement leaders can map upstream and midstream suppliers, uncovering hidden risks before they escalate into critical disruptions. ![image of two people looking at a computer screen](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20701%20672'%2F%3E) Identify and mitigate vulnerabilities with a comprehensive view of supplier relationships and dependencies across your network. By reducing blind spots, improving data accuracy, and providing real-time risk insights, organizations can stay ahead of supplier and supply chain disruptions, compliance issues, and reputational threats. ## Beyond visibility: Gain *N*-Tier transparency Seeing your Tier 2–3 suppliers is just the beginning, true *N*-Tier transparency requires accurate, reliable data and a comprehensive view of supplier relationships. While many organizations believe they have visibility beyond Tier 1, gaps in data and insights leave them vulnerable to hidden risks across their supply networks. With Sphera’s holistic *N*-Tier solution, organizations can proactively address disruptions, regulatory compliance issues, and reputational threats, ensuring risk mitigation strategies are comprehensive. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Get Full Visibility of All Corporate and Operational Risks ](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20721%20721'%2F%3E) ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20721%20721'%2F%3E) ## Enhancing Supplier Engagement The number of *N*-Tier solutions available to corporations to manage and improve the Tier 2-3 supplier visibility is growing exponentially. Unfortunately, managing them has become a resource-intensive balancing act involving unverified data and generic high-volume unmanageable lists and a lack of actionable intelligence. The Southeast Michigan region is comprised of Livingston, Macomb, Monroe, Oakland, St. Clair, Washtenaw, and Wayne Counties. The region is 4,600 square miles and has a population of 4.8 million people. SEMCOG is enabled by Act 281, P.A. 1945 as amended. The organization’s bylaws were adopted in June of 1967, and the organization began operation in 1968. Slips, trips and falls account for a significant proportion of workplace injuries. Mine operators need to manage risks like uneven surfaces, loose gravel, debris and slippery surfaces. Miners are particularly vulnerable when walking on wet walkways, climbing onto equipment, or navigating poorly lit areas. These risks are compounded by human factors such as fatigue, distraction and improper footwear, as well as equipment factors like poorly maintained access points and lack of anti-slip features. To mitigate these hazards, mining companies must prioritize regular maintenance of walkways, ensure proper lighting, and provide training on hazard recognition and safe navigation. The use of non-slip footwear and traction devices is essential, especially during winter months. Leaders play a critical role by celebrating proactive hazard mitigation — such as shoveling snow, applying ice melt, and staging safety materials for easy access. Effective workplace exams, job risk assessments, and equipment inspections are key to identifying and minimizing risks. Electricity is a key component of the fabric of modern society and the Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) Enterprise serves to strengthen that fabric. The vision for the ERO Enterprise, which is comprised of NERC and the six Regional Entities, is a highly reliable, resilient, and secure North American bulk power system (BPS). Our mission is to assure the effective and efficient reduction of risks to the reliability and security of the grid. Reliability | Resilience | Security Because nearly 400 million citizens in North America are counting on us The North American BPS is made up of six Regional Entities as shown on the map and in the corresponding table below. The multicolored area denotes overlap as some load-serving entities participate in one Regional Entity while associated Transmission Owners/Operators participate in another. MRO Midwest Reliability Organization NPCC Northeast Power Coordinating Council RF ReliabilityFirst SERC SERC Reliability Corporation Texas RE Texas Reliability Entity WECC WECC 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment 4 About This Assessment NERC is a not-for-profit international regulatory authority with the mission to assure the reliability of the BPS in North America. NERC develops and enforces Reliability Standards; annually assesses seasonal and long-term reliability; monitors the BPS through system awareness; and educates, trains, and certifies industry personnel. NERC’s area of responsibility spans the continental United States, Canada, and the northern portion of Baja California, Mexico. NERC is the ERO for North America and is subject to oversight by the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC, also known as the Commission) and governmental authorities in Canada. NERC’s jurisdiction includes users, owners, and operators of the North American BPS and serves more than 334 million people. Section 39.11(b) of FERC’s regulations provides that “The Electric Reliability Organization shall conduct assessments of the adequacy of the Bulk‐Power System in North America and report its findings to the Commission, the Secretary of Energy, each Regional Entity, and each Regional Advisory Body annually or more frequently if so ordered by the Commission.” The Long-Term Reliability Assessment (LTRA), along with NERC’s other reliability assessments and analysis reports, supports the ERO Enterprise vision and mission by providing independent analysis of reliability risks. Other important assessments and reports include the following: • Seasonal Reliability Assessments: The Summer Reliability Assessment (SRA) and Winter Reliability Assessment (WRA) provide overall perspective on the adequacy of the generation resources and the transmission systems necessary to meet projected seasonal peak demands. They also identify reliability issues of interest and areas of concern for the upcoming season. Seasonal assessments are published annually prior to each respective season. • Special Reliability Assessments: In addition to the long-term and seasonal reliability assessments, NERC also conducts special reliability assessments on a regional, interregional, and Interconnection basis as conditions warrant, or as requested by the NERC Board of Trustees or governmental authorities. Special reliability assessments are performed and published on an as-needed basis. • State of Reliability Report (SOR): The SOR contains an unbiased, data-driven look at BPS reliability for the calendar year, identifying ongoing challenges and informing future-looking reliability assessments. It seeks to inform regulators, policymakers, and industry leaders of the most significant reliability risks facing the BPS and describe the actions that the ERO 1 NERC Rules of Procedure - Section 803 2 Section 39.11(b) of FERC’s regulations states the following: “The Electric Reliability Organization shall conduct assessments of the adequacy of the Bulk-Power System in North America and report its findings to the Commission, the Secretary of Energy, each Regional Entity, and each Regional Advisory Body annually or more frequently if so ordered by the Commission.” Enterprise has taken, and will take, to address them. The SOR is published annually, containing analysis of BPS performance data from the prior year. • Event Analysis Reports: NERC publishes reports of major system events and off-normal system occurrences as one output of the ERO Event Analysis Program. This program employs rigorous post-event analysis and promotes broad understanding of the causes and effects of reliability events. NERC also publishes Lessons Learned for industry. Reliability assessments and analysis are published on NERC’s website. Title: Tier 2 Supplier Mapping: 7 Steps to Secure Your Supply Chain 2026
Raw_Content_Text: [Skip to content](#content) [![imexdbusinesslogo](https://imexdbusiness.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/imexdbussines_logo-768x106.jpg)](https://imexdbusiness.com/home-new/) [Go to ImexReports](https://imexreports.imexdbusiness.com/login) # Tier 2 Supplier Mapping: 7 Steps to Secure Your Supply Chain ![Tier 2 supplier mapping](https://imexdbusiness.com/wp-content/uploads/elementor/thumbs/unnamed-file-4-rimvcyopd2unzp6wjjcth0n88s2xh8pna58wxdzjpk.webp "unnamed-file-4") Your primary supplier just confirmed your next shipment is on schedule. But what if *their* critical raw material provider is on the verge of a labor strike you know nothing about? This hidden vulnerability is where supply chains break, and it’s why mastering **Tier 2 supplier mapping** is no longer optional for leaders in India and Asia; it’s your primary defense for 2026. ## Why Your Current Supplier View Is Dangerously Incomplete For years, managing direct (Tier 1) suppliers was the gold standard. My experience advising dozens of manufacturing and retail giants across Asia has shown me one consistent truth: the most damaging disruptions originate from the suppliers you don’t see. A recent [Bain & Company report](https://www.thebci.org/news/supply-chain-disruptions-drive-increased-tier-mapping-and-insurance-uptake.html) confirms that 81% of companies faced at least one major supply chain disruption last year. Relying solely on your Tier 1 relationships is like driving a high-speed vehicle by only looking at the dashboard; you’re completely blind to the road ahead. The supply chain ecosystems in India, Vietnam, and across Southeast Asia are uniquely complex—a layered network of specialized SMEs, regional distributors, and family-owned operations. This diversity is a strength, but it also creates significant opacity. Without deep *indirect supplier visibility*, you are unknowingly exposed to geopolitical shifts, local regulatory changes, and financial instability one, two, or even three tiers down your value chain. This is a level of risk no modern business can afford to ignore. ## The 7 Steps to Master Tier 2 Supplier Mapping Moving from reactive problem-solving to proactive resilience requires a structured methodology. Based on my work building secure supply chains, this seven-step process provides a clear path to achieving the visibility you need. This is the core of effective supply chain risk management. ### Step 1: Identify and Prioritize Critical Tier 1 Suppliers You cannot map everything at once. Begin by identifying your most critical Tier 1 suppliers. Focus on those who provide components essential for your highest-revenue products or those who are single-source vendors. Analyze your spend data and production dependencies to create a prioritized list. This focus ensures your initial efforts have the greatest impact on business continuity. ### Step 2: Leverage Data for Indirect Supplier Identification This is where you move beyond conversations and into hard data. Your Tier 1 suppliers may be hesitant or simply unable to provide a complete list of their own vendors. This is where a robust **company intelligence platform** built on foreign trade data becomes indispensable. By analyzing your Tier 1 supplier’s verified import and export records using a tool like our *Imex-reports*, you can directly see who they are doing business with. This objective data trail is the fastest and most reliable way to begin your *indirect supplier identification* process. ### Step 3: Conduct an Initial Risk Assessment Once you have a preliminary list of Tier 2 suppliers, conduct a high-level risk assessment. Look for immediate red flags. Are they located in a region prone to natural disasters or political instability? Are there public records of financial trouble or labor disputes? This initial screening helps you focus your deeper due diligence efforts where they are most needed. ### Step 4: Foster Collaborative Transparency with Tier 1 Partners Approach your Tier 1 suppliers as partners in risk mitigation, not subjects of an audit. Share your rationale and explain that strengthening the entire chain benefits everyone. A 2023 Deloitte survey revealed that only 22% of organizations actively monitor risks beyond their direct suppliers. Frame this initiative as a competitive advantage that you are building together, increasing their value as a strategic partner. ### Step 5: Perform Deep Vetting on High-Risk Tier 2 Suppliers For the Tier 2 suppliers identified as high-risk, it’s time for a deeper dive. This *sub-tier vendor analysis* must go beyond basic financials. Use customs and trade data to verify their operational history, shipment volumes, and other key business partners. Cross-referencing this information helps you validate their stability and importance within the broader network, a core function of an effective market opportunity analysis. ### Step 6: Create Your Supply Chain Network Visualization Knowledge in a spreadsheet is static. True understanding comes from visualization. Use software or platforms to map the connections between your company, your Tier 1 suppliers, and their Tier 2 suppliers. This **supply chain network visualization** makes it easy to spot concentration risks—like multiple Tier 1 partners depending on the same single Tier 2 component manufacturer. Seeing these hidden dependencies is often the most eye-opening part of the process. ### Step 7: Implement Continuous Monitoring and Alerts Tier 2 supplier mapping is not a one-time project; it’s an ongoing discipline. Set up automated monitoring using real-time data feeds. Gartner predicts that by 2026, over 50% of large enterprises will have invested in real-time visibility platforms. You need alerts for events like shipping delays from a Tier 2 supplier’s port, negative news mentions, or changes in their trade patterns. This transforms your strategy from historical analysis to proactive, real-time intervention, which is essential when dealing with [global supply chain bottlenecks](https://imexdbusiness.com/global-supply-chain-bottlenecks-real-time-data/). ## From Risk Mitigation to Strategic Advantage True mastery of Tier 2 visibility extends beyond merely preventing disasters. It creates tangible business opportunities. With this deeper intelligence, you can enhance your ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) compliance by ensuring your sub-tier suppliers meet ethical standards—a critical factor as regulations like India’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) become more stringent. This deep insight into complex networks, such as the [automotive supply chain](https://imexdbusiness.com/automotive-supply-chain-data-ev-sourcing/), allows you to identify innovative component manufacturers or alternative material sources before your competitors do, creating a significant strategic advantage. ## Your Actionable Framework for Getting Started Translating this strategy into action requires focus. As a seasoned consultant, I advise my clients to begin with these three concrete steps: * **Launch a Pilot Project:** Select one critical product line or a single strategic Tier 1 supplier. Run through the entire 7-step mapping process for this focused group. This creates a quick win, demonstrates value to stakeholders, and provides a template for a full-scale rollout. * **Establish a Cross-Functional Team:** Your supply chain team cannot do this alone. Create a dedicated team with members from procurement, compliance, and finance. This ensures all facets of supplier risk—from operational to financial to regulatory—are properly evaluated, which is a cornerstone of any effective [trade compliance audit](https://imexdbusiness.com/trade-compliance-audit-guide-india/). * **Invest in a Centralized Data Platform:** Relying on emails and spreadsheets is a recipe for failure. You need a single source of truth. A platform that integrates customs data, corporate firmographics, and risk alerts is the engine that powers a modern, resilient supply chain strategy. This is precisely what Imex-reports is built to deliver. ## Illuminate Your Blind Spots and Secure Your Future The conversation around supply chain management has fundamentally shifted. It’s no longer about managing relationships; it’s about managing complex, interconnected networks. The blind spots in your Tier 2 and beyond represent the single greatest threat to your revenue and reputation. By implementing a robust **Tier 2 supplier mapping** program, you move from a position of vulnerability to one of control and strategic foresight. You transform risk into resilience. See how Imex-reports can illuminate your entire supply chain, revealing the risks and opportunities hidden within. **[Request your personalized demo today](https://imexdbusiness.com/imexreports/)** and take the first step towards true supply chain security. ### Want to obtain more information? Title: Stellantis's Recall and Its Implications for EV Supply Chain Resilience
Raw_Content_Text: ![logo](data:image/png;base64,) [News](/news/)/ [Consumer Discretionary](/news/sector/consumer-discretionary/)/ [STLA](/news/stock/NYSE-STLA/)/ Articles Details # Stellantis's Recall and Its Implications for EV Supply Chain Resilience ![Speaker 1](https://cdn.ainvest.com/articles/focusnews/coverimage/content/pictures/en_chris_2e9da4cb1755765022745.png) ![Speaker 2](https://cdn.ainvest.com/articles/focusnews/coverimage/content/pictures/alexander_9990f0971755765042310.png) ![Aime Robot](https://cdn.ainvest.com/frontResources/s/nova-ainews/news/_next/static/media/aimeRobot.ddb9bcda.png) - [Stellantis](https://chart.ainvest.com/NYSE-STLA/)[STLA--](//www.ainvest.com/stocks/NYSE-STLA/) recalled 320,000 Jeep plug-in hybrids due to battery fire risks, exposing supply chain vulnerabilities linked to supplier misalignment and technical flaws. - The recall triggered a 15% stock drop for battery supplier [Novonix](https://chart.ainvest.com/NASDAQ-NVX/)[NVX--](//www.ainvest.com/stocks/NASDAQ-NVX/), highlighting systemic risks in EV ecosystems reliant on niche suppliers for critical components. - Stellantis is diversifying suppliers and partnering with Factorial Energy (solid-state batteries) and CATL (LFP batteries) to strengthen resilience while investing $13B in U.S. manufacturing. - These strategic moves aim to balance electrification with traditional tech, addressing regulatory uncertainties and consumer preferences through dual-chemistry battery strategies and domestic production. - For investors, the case underscores that EV success requires supply chain agility, technological innovation, and geopolitical risk management to navigate systemic industry transformation. ### The Recall and Supply Chain Vulnerabilities A [Bloomberg report](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-11-04/stellantis-recalls-320-000-hybrid-jeep-models-in-us-on-fire-risk) found that the affected Jeep Wrangler and Grand Cherokee plug-in hybrids (2020–2025 models) were recalled due to battery packs built with cells susceptible to separator damage, a flaw that could lead to thermal runaway and fires. Stellantis's decision to terminate its offtake agreement with Novonix-a battery materials supplier-further highlights the fragility of supplier relationships in complex EV ecosystems; [MarketScreener](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/automaker-stellantis-scraps-supply-deal-with-australia-s-novonix-ce7d5cded888f221) reported the move and the subsequent 15% plunge in Novonix's stock. This episode illustrates a broader challenge: the automotive supply chain's reliance on niche suppliers for critical components like battery materials. When technical or operational misalignments occur, the consequences ripple across the value chain, from reputational damage to financial losses. For Stellantis, the recall not only disrupted customer trust but also exposed the risks of over-concentration in supplier partnerships. ### Strategic Responses to Enhance Resilience In response to such vulnerabilities, Stellantis has embarked on a multifaceted strategy to strengthen its EV supply chain. A key pillar is supplier diversification. While the termination of the [Novonix](https://chart.ainvest.com/NASDAQ-NVX/)[NVX--](//www.ainvest.com/stocks/NASDAQ-NVX/) deal was a setback, [Novonix said](https://www.novonixgroup.com/news/novonix-and-stellantis-sign-binding-offtake-agreement/) it later signed a binding offtake agreement with the automaker for 115,000 tonnes of synthetic graphite over six years, starting in 2026. This dual approach-both terminating and re-engaging with Novonix-reflects a calculated effort to balance risk mitigation with long-term resource security. Equally significant are Stellantis's partnerships in battery technology. [Stellantis and Factorial Energy](https://www.stellantis.com/en/news/press-releases/2025/april/stellantis-and-factorial-energy-reach-key-milestone-in-solid-state-battery-development) have validated automotive-sized solid-state battery cells with an energy density of 375Wh/kg, a breakthrough that could redefine EV performance and safety. These batteries, capable of operating in extreme temperatures and offering faster charging times, are slated for integration into a demonstration fleet by 2026. Meanwhile, the [CATL joint venture](https://www.stellantis.com/en/news/press-releases/2024/december/stellantis-and-calt-to-invest-up-to-4-1-billion-in-joint-venture-for-large-scale-lfp-battery-plant-in-spain) to build a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant in Spain-backed by up to €4.1 billion-underscores Stellantis's dual-chemistry strategy, ensuring flexibility in meeting diverse market demands. Domestically, [Stellantis announced](https://www.stellantis.com/en/news/press-releases/2025/october/stellantis-to-invest-13-billion-to-grow-in-the-united-states) a $13 billion investment to bolster its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a range-extended EV and a new internal combustion engine large SUV set to launch in 2028. These investments, coupled with a $100 million commitment to Kokomo, Indiana, for advanced powertrain development, signal a pragmatic approach to balancing electrification with traditional technologies. Such diversification is critical in navigating regulatory uncertainties and shifting consumer preferences. ![](https://cdn.ainvest.com/aigc/hxcmp/images/compress-qwen_generated_1762250889329.jpg.png?format=webp&width=700) ![](https://cdn.ainvest.com/aigc/hxcmp/images/compress-qwen_generated_1762250889329.jpg.png?format=webp&width=700) ### Investment Implications: Risks and Opportunities For investors, Stellantis's journey highlights two key themes. First, supply chain resilience is no longer a peripheral concern but a core determinant of competitive advantage. The recall and subsequent supplier adjustments demonstrate that even well-capitalized automakers are vulnerable to systemic shocks. [Supply Chain Management Review](https://www.scmr.com/article/turning-vehicle-recalls-into-a-test-of-supply-chain-resilience-lessons-from-2025) noted that leading OEMs are increasingly adopting cross-functional crisis teams and predictive risk modeling to preempt bottlenecks. Stellantis's investments in these areas-such as optimizing pack architecture and securing dual-chemistry battery capacity-position it to outperform peers in recall management and customer retention. Second, the automaker's partnerships with cutting-edge battery firms like Factorial Energy and CATL represent high-stakes opportunities. Solid-state batteries, if commercialized successfully, could reduce dependency on lithium and cobalt while enhancing vehicle range and safety. However, such innovations require sustained R&D spending and regulatory approvals, introducing execution risks. Similarly, the CATL joint venture, while promising, hinges on geopolitical stability and European market dynamics. ### Conclusion Stellantis's recall and its aftermath serve as a microcosm of the broader challenges facing the EV industry. While supply chain disruptions and technical flaws pose immediate risks, the automaker's strategic pivot toward diversification, technological collaboration, and domestic investment offers a roadmap for long-term resilience. For investors, the lesson is clear: electrification is not merely a technological shift but a systemic transformation that demands agility, foresight, and a willingness to navigate complexity. In this evolving landscape, companies that balance innovation with supply chain robustness will emerge as leaders-and Stellantis's actions suggest it is striving to be one. ![author avatar](https://cdn.ainvest.com/social/account/portraits/albert.png?format=webp&width=48&height=48) AI Writing Agent Albert Fox. Raw_Content_Text: ![en flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/us.svg) ![English flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/us.svg) ![German flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/de.svg) ![Sphera Logo](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo.png)![Sphera Logo (White Version)](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![Sphera Logo (White Version)](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![sphera logo](/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![1@2x-1-1](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/1@2x-1-1.png) # Sub-Tier Visibility Sub-tier Visibility visualizes the process of monitoring and alerting n-tier supply chains within Sphera SCRM. With supplier-validated supply sites, you can confidently map sub-tier dependencies and more accurately expose threats in your sub-tiers before they become critical. Collaborate with suppliers for end-to-end visibility. Receive indicator messages and alerts concerning direct suppliers as well as sub-tier suppliers; visualize supply chain dependencies on a digital world map; and reveal risky situations across multiple tiers so you can drive better decisions earlier ### Get full visibility of all corporate and operational risks Managing company risks in one central application enables you to rapidly initiate complete, coordinated responses. Your team can identify key factors quickly because contextual data is automatically populated, keeping data entry to a minimum. The solution is designed to enable specificity, speed and focus. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Get Full Visibility of All Corporate and Operational Risks ](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20721%20721'%2F%3E) ### Automated invitation process By inviting your tier-1 suppliers to join Supply Risk Network, your suppliers can securely share their supplier information, so everyone gains true visibility into the joint multi-tier supply network. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Automated invitation process](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20721%20721'%2F%3E) ### Verified sub-tier relations Transparency into tier-1 supplier sites, supply paths to tier 2, and tier-2 supplier locations provide accurate multi-tier transparency. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Verified Sub Tier Relations’](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20721%20721'%2F%3E) ## Benefits Supply chain resiliency By inviting suppliers to participate and share data within Supply Risk Network, you enable them to be more risk aware. Save time & money Automated time-consuming manual collection of risk information. Avoid contractual fines and penalties from missed deliveries. Extended value Gaining multi-tier risk insights lets you extend the value of Sphera SCRM for risk tracking, alerts, and mitigation at the sub-tier level, so you do understand the criticality of risk events in your sub-tiers. This reduces the cost of mitigating risk and helps keep production lines running. Identify risk sooner By gaining visibility of risk throughout multiple tiers of your supply base, you can identify risk sooner. You can react faster and reduce bottlenecks through collaborative visualization of your sub-tier risk exposure. ![Navigating supply chains in an ESG world end page](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20711%20499'%2F%3E) ## Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report 2024 We are pleased to introduce the inaugural Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report. This report explores the top five risks faced by enterprises and suppliers in 2023, as well as their causes and consequences. ## Our Awards ![Sphera Branding Logo](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2054%2080'%2F%3E) ### Artificial Intelligence Stratus Award for Artificial Intelligence or Cloud Computing 2023 [Learn More](#) ![Sustainability 2024 – Sphera’s ESG Focus](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%2086%2080'%2F%3E) ### Sustainability Leader Spend Matters 50 Procurement Providers to Know 2022 [Learn More](#) ![Corporate ESG Strategy](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20140%2066'%2F%3E) ### Top Product World Procurement Leaders Highly Commended Technology Innovation 2022 [Learn More](#) ![Clip path group](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%2032'%2F%3E) ### Green Quadrant ProcureTech 100 Risk Management 2022 [Learn More](#) ![clariant_331x100](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20300%2091'%2F%3E) ###### Global Supply Risk Manager, Clariant “The company that has visibility into its sub-tiers has a big advantage over its competitors. You hear about disruption first, so you’re the first to react.” ![agco-331×100](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20300%2091'%2F%3E) ###### Senior VP Global Purchasing and Materials Management AGCO Corporation “Thanks to Sphera Supply Chain Risk Management [formerly riskmethods] we instantly saw which of our suppliers were impacted when the Coronavirus hit northern Italy. This allowed us to switch to alternative sources before our competition to ensure business continuity.” ## Request a demo Fill out the form and we will get back to you to discuss your sub-tier visibility needs. ###### ## Resources ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%201996%201496'%2F%3E) #### Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report 2026 ![](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%207721%205150'%2F%3E) #### AI-Powered Supplier Risk Management Survey 2025 ![aerial view of container ship](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%201422%20800'%2F%3E) #### Future-Proofing Supply Chains: AI as a Risk Management Game Changer ### Explore the modules in this suite Our enterprise-wide, fully integrated software reduces the likelihood of incidents and operational losses. Risk Radar Leverage the power of AI to map and proactively protect your supply network. Impact Analyzer Assess the criticality of suppliers and detect vulnerabilities. Content_Snippet: Title: Hyundai’s Georgia EV supplier network adds 3 more manufacturers | WardsAuto # Hyundai’s Georgia EV supplier network adds 3 more manufacturers. South Korea-based DAS Corp., an automotive parts supplier, will produce automotive seat structures for the upcoming Hyundai EV metacampus as well as other automakers in North America. Three Hyundai suppliers plan to add manufacturing plants in Georgia for a combined investment of nearly $180 million, according to a series of announcements from Gov. Brian Kemp. Automotive parts manufacturer NVH Korea will invest over $72 million in a new manufacturing facility in Locust Grove, Georgia, according to a June state release. The Locust Grove plant will be the company’s second Georgia facility. The company will produce luggage boards and covers and is also a supplier for General Motors and Kia, the latter of which also has a manufacturing facility in West Point. In July, Kia announced it was investing $200 million to expand the plant to produce its new electric SUV model beginning in Q2 of next year. are the latest suppliers to build an auto parts manufacturing plant near Hyundai’s EV Metaplant campus. The three factories follow Hyundai to the state after the automaker announced a $5.5 billion manufacturing campus in Ellabell last year, the largest economic development project in Georgia’s history. “Suppliers for the Hyundai Metaplant resulted in over $2 billion in investment last fiscal year alone, helping Georgia achieve a third straight year of record-breaking economic growth,” Kemp said in a statement last week. Hyundai has also been investing heavily in itself regarding its upcoming $5.5 billion EV metaplant. In late May, Hyundai and LG Energy Solution struck a joint venture deal to build a $4.3 billion battery cell plant, which will be adjacent to the automaker’s EV campus. But at the beginning of September, the two companies announced it was investing $2 billion more toward the upcoming plant. The two South Korea-based companies will each take a 50% stake in the venture and facility, where Hyundai will assemble battery packs using cells from the plant to be sent to its U.S. manufacturing sites. * LG Energy, Hyundai to invest additional $2B in Georgia battery cell plant. * Hyundai’s Georgia supplier network expands to 9 manufacturers.

The report is an output of the Clean Energy Ministerial Hydrogen Initiative and is intended to inform energy sector stakeholders on the status and future prospects of hydrogen. Focusing on hydrogen’s potential role in meeting international energy and climate goals, the Review aims to help decision makers fine-tune strategies to attract investment and facilitate deployment of hydrogen technologies at the same time as creating demand for hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels. It compares real-world developments with the stated ambitions of government and industry. This year’s report has a special focus on Latin America and includes analysis on recent developments of low-emissions hydrogen projects in the region and how to unlock demand and move towards project implementation. In addition, the report assesses in detail the greenhouse gas emissions associated with different hydrogen supply chains. I EA. CC BY 4.0. Raw_Content_Text: ![en flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/us.svg) ![English flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/us.svg) ![German flag](/wp-content/plugins/sitepress-multilingual-cms/res/flags/de.svg) ![Sphera Logo](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo.png)![Sphera Logo (White Version)](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![Sphera Logo (White Version)](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![sphera logo](/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/sphera-logo-white.png) ![1@2x-1-1](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/1@2x-1-1.png) # Sub-Tier Visibility Sub-tier Visibility visualizes the process of monitoring and alerting n-tier supply chains within Sphera SCRM. With supplier-validated supply sites, you can confidently map sub-tier dependencies and more accurately expose threats in your sub-tiers before they become critical. Collaborate with suppliers for end-to-end visibility. Receive indicator messages and alerts concerning direct suppliers as well as sub-tier suppliers; visualize supply chain dependencies on a digital world map; and reveal risky situations across multiple tiers so you can drive better decisions earlier ### Get full visibility of all corporate and operational risks Managing company risks in one central application enables you to rapidly initiate complete, coordinated responses. Your team can identify key factors quickly because contextual data is automatically populated, keeping data entry to a minimum. The solution is designed to enable specificity, speed and focus. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Get Full Visibility of All Corporate and Operational Risks ](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Get-Full-Visibility-of-All-Corporate-and-Operational-Risks-.webp) ### Automated invitation process By inviting your tier-1 suppliers to join Supply Risk Network, your suppliers can securely share their supplier information, so everyone gains true visibility into the joint multi-tier supply network. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Automated invitation process](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Automated-invitation-process-.webp) ### Verified sub-tier relations Transparency into tier-1 supplier sites, supply paths to tier 2, and tier-2 supplier locations provide accurate multi-tier transparency. ![SCRM Module Graphics_Sub Tier Visibility – Verified Sub Tier Relations’](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SCRM-Module-Graphics_Sub-Tier-Visibility-Verified-Sub-Tier-Relations.webp) ## Benefits Supply chain resiliency By inviting suppliers to participate and share data within Supply Risk Network, you enable them to be more risk aware. Save time & money Automated time-consuming manual collection of risk information. Avoid contractual fines and penalties from missed deliveries. Extended value Gaining multi-tier risk insights lets you extend the value of Sphera SCRM for risk tracking, alerts, and mitigation at the sub-tier level, so you do understand the criticality of risk events in your sub-tiers. This reduces the cost of mitigating risk and helps keep production lines running. Identify risk sooner By gaining visibility of risk throughout multiple tiers of your supply base, you can identify risk sooner. You can react faster and reduce bottlenecks through collaborative visualization of your sub-tier risk exposure. ![Navigating supply chains in an ESG world end page](https://sphera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Navigating-supply-chains-in-an-ESG-world-end-page.webp) ## Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report 2024 We are pleased to introduce the inaugural Sphera Supply Chain Risk Report. Title: Hyundai’s Georgia EV supplier network adds 3 more manufacturers | Manufacturing Dive
Content_Snippet: Title: Hyundai’s Georgia EV supplier network adds 3 more manufacturers | Manufacturing Dive # Hyundai’s Georgia EV supplier network adds 3 more manufacturers. South Korea-based DAS Corp., an automotive parts supplier, will produce automotive seat structures for the upcoming Hyundai EV metacampus as well as other automakers in North America. Three Hyundai suppliers plan to add manufacturing plants in Georgia for a combined investment of nearly $180 million, according to a series of announcements from Gov. Brian Kemp. Automotive parts manufacturer NVH Korea will invest over $72 million in a new manufacturing facility in Locust Grove, Georgia, according to a June state release. The company will produce luggage boards and covers and is also a supplier for General Motors and Kia, the latter of which also has a manufacturing facility in West Point. In July, Kia announced it was investing $200 million to expand the plant to produce its new electric SUV model beginning in Q2 of next year. are the latest suppliers to build an auto parts manufacturing plant near Hyundai’s EV Metaplant campus. The three factories follow Hyundai to the state after the automaker announced a $5.5 billion manufacturing campus in Ellabell last year, the largest economic development project in Georgia’s history. “Suppliers for the Hyundai Metaplant resulted in over $2 billion in investment last fiscal year alone, helping Georgia achieve a third straight year of record-breaking economic growth,” Kemp said in a statement last week. Hyundai has also been investing heavily in itself regarding its upcoming $5.5 billion EV metaplant. In late May, Hyundai and LG Energy Solution struck a joint venture deal to build a $4.3 billion battery cell plant, which will be adjacent to the automaker’s EV campus. But at the beginning of September, the two companies announced it was investing $2 billion more toward the upcoming plant. The two South Korea-based companies will each take a 50% stake in the venture and facility, where Hyundai will assemble battery packs using cells from the plant to be sent to its U.S. manufacturing sites. The total $6.3 billion investment will create 8,500 jobs, a state official told Manufacturing Dive in an email. * LG Energy, Hyundai to invest additional $2B in Georgia battery cell plant. * Hyundai’s Georgia supplier network expands to 9 manufacturers.

Title: [PDF] GRIDOVATION - Georgia Transmission
Raw_Content_Text: 2 0 2 4 A N N U A L R E P O R T GRIDOVATION Investing Today for a Brighter Tomorrow As technology advances, it takes more energy to power homes, fuel industries and generate economic prosperity. Georgia Transmission’s Gridovation is a historic investment in energy infrastructure to ensure Georgia communities have access to resilient, cost-effective power you can rely on today, tomorrow and beyond. Contents 3 Financial and Operating Highlights 5 A Message from our Officers 7  For the Moments that Count 9  More than Innovation 11  Financial Stewardship 13 People-Centric Energy 15 Member Systems 16 Board of Directors 17 Executive Management Team 18 Financial Information Georgia Transmission partners with 38 electric membership corporations (EMCs) to deliver energy to more than 4.7 million Georgians across 70% of the state’s land area. Together, we’re always moving forward to meet Georgia’s ever-growing need for safe, reliable and cost-effective electricity. 2 Back to Contents 3 Back to Contents Financial and Operating Highlights (dollars in thousands) Total Assets $3,896,618 Total Operating Revenues $ 447,494 Net Margin $ 40,072 Patronage Capital and $ 450,070 Membership Fees (dollars in thousands) Transmission Lines $1,608,636 Distribution Substations $ 792,951 Transmission Substations $ 654,515 General Plant $ 69,403 Plant Held for Future Use $ 34,435 $1,608,636 Transmission Lines $792,951 Distribution Substations $654,515 Transmission Substations $69,403 General Plant $34,435 Plant Held for Future Use 4 Back to Contents 5 Back to Contents At Georgia Transmission, we believe progress is only made when you keep pushing forward. That’s why we ask our talented team of problem-solvers to bring their biggest and most innovative ideas to the table every day. As we look to the future of energy, we know it’s going to take more than a step of progress at a time to keep meeting the growing energy demands of our community. So, instead of steps, we’re asking our team to take leaps. That is why in 2024 we launched Gridovation, our multiyear innovation and grid investment initiative. By making consistent investments and leading with innovative solutions, we’re positioning ourselves to continue to deliver on our mission of providing the best in reliable, cost-effective service our members expect, and on which millions of Georgians rely. In 2024, this meant Georgia Transmission: •  Invested $669 million, completing 104 capital projects, including a historic purchase of existing assets to support parity in the Integrated Transmission System (ITS) and the construction of new facilities to support commercial/industrial customer-choice loads for our member systems; •  Advanced approximately $602 million on a Rural Utility Service (RUS) loan for post-construction funding of transmission projects; •  Awaiting final approval for a $244 million loan from the Federal Financing Bank (FFB) for strategic operational support and post-construction funding of transmission projects; •  Continued to monitor cybersecurity developments and comply with federal reliability standards; •  Incurred no environmental violations for the 11th consecutive year; and •  Maintained a focus on safety, health and well-being. In addition to these current year investments, we also took steps to ready our business for the demands of tomorrow: •  We moved to new corporate headquarters, adding space for collaboration and room to support our evolving workforce needs. •  We received approval for additional funding from federal grant programs that will allow us to deploy new technology and infrastructure to support greater grid resiliency. •  We continued to expand our business intelligence program, bot-automation activities and knowledge-transfer initiative to ensure we are leveraging the best of technology and data to work efficiently and bridge our workforce transition. •  We launched innovative internal programs, such as our Ask GTC chatbot, aimed at streamlining common, everyday tasks. •  Additionally, we participated in an audit of our safety programs, ensuring we continue to put the safety of our people and those with whom we interact first in everything we do. A Message from our Officers 6 Back to Contents We believe the best progress happens when we solve problems collaboratively – that principle is something we’ve held true to since our inception in 1997. We put this into practice every day by partnering with our 38 member systems to meet their unique needs, and, together, we deliver the safe, reliable and cost-effective electricity that helps add light to the stories of more than 4.7 million Georgians. We look forward to sharing more details about these milestones, our continued financial strength and strategic initiatives in the pages ahead. Steve Rawl Sr. Vice Chairman Otis P. Jones Secretary-Treasurer Charles R. Fendley Chairman 7 Back to Contents For the Moments that Count Today, having electricity at the flip of a switch goes without thought as we move through our daily routines. At Georgia Transmission, we like the thought of that –– it means that together, with our members, we’re reliably keeping your stories illuminated. Sometimes Mother Nature likes to challenge that standard of reliability, but our dedicated teams of associates and partners are always willing to answer that challenge. In September, Hurricane Helene carved a path of destruction throughout the Southeast. In Georgia, we saw the storm’s devastating impacts from Valdosta to Augusta, and everywhere in between. For many, Hurricane Helene brought back memories of Hurricanes Irma and Michael. For others, the devastation from this storm was unrelatable to anything their areas of the state had seen. At the peak of the storm, our members saw more than 435,000 EMC members without power. This rivaled the record of 550,000 EMC outages Hurricane Irma caused. For Georgia Transmission, at the peak of the storm, we had 152 transmission lines out, with another 62 lines that experienced some momentary outages. We also had 196 EMC load-serving substations offline at one time –– roughly a quarter of our substations. Despite the devastation, the restoration was swift. Our teams jumped into action in the wake of Hurricane Helene’s destruction Sept. 26 to have all our substations and transmission lines restored by Oct. 4. We then shifted our resources to support our members in their efforts to restore power to the homes and businesses that could safely receive electricity. The response to Hurricane Helene exemplified the cooperative difference. Our associates call communities throughout Georgia home, and many opened their homes and kitchens to be places of respite to line crews, colleagues and others responding to the storm. Our support teams worked around the clock to help remove the logistical barriers our field teams were experiencing –– from needing access to fuel and navigating communication outages to finding food and shelter. Additionally, Hurricane Helene put our training and technology investments to the test. We were able to showcase the success of our investment in grid monitoring and automation technology. We also highlighted the nimbleness of our team, which comes as the result of their expertise and consistent training. While those actions helped our restoration time, having the goal of being better every day means there’s no finish line in our opportunity for improvements. To that end, our associates took a retrospective look to find opportunities to be better prepared. As a result, our research and development teams are looking at new technology that could help our field associates remain better connected in disaster situations. We’re also partnering with our members to make sure we’re working even closer together to better benefit from each other’s expertise. And, we’re continuing our investments in new and emerging technology that adds greater grid resiliency. 8 Back to Contents Georgia’s EMCs joined with crews from other states to make repairs to the distribution system after Hurricane Helene. Tent cities were set up around the state to support the numerous crews that made the repairs. 9 Back to Contents Meeting the complex energy demands of tomorrow will take more than just pursuing traditional infrastructure, it will require an innovative leap forward. That’s why we launched our Gridovation initiative in 2024. This initiative is a significant, multiyear investment in energy infrastructure to ensure communities across Georgia have access to resilient, cost-effective power they can rely on today, tomorrow and beyond. Using this initiative to renew our always forward-thinking mindset, we’re taking time to explore and implement new technology throughout our system. And, in 2024, we already saw some innovative ideas add light. In the summer, we commissioned our Middle Fork SVS. This dynamic system is designed to help ensure the power grid continues to deliver resilient and quality electricity throughout north Georgia. With the addition of more low-inertia energy sources to the generation mix, more generation being based in south Georgia and the demand for energy continuing to grow in the northern part of the state, voltage and power quality could become an issue in north Georgia. The technology we deployed with the Middle Fork SVS works as a safety net to prevent those issues from occurring. The technology goes by many names –– STATCom, static synchronous compensator or simply static var system, but the magic it produces is all the same. The Middle Fork SVS makes sure the voltage is not too low and not too high. It injects reactive power (vars) to raise the voltage, and it can absorb reactive power from the transmission system to lower the voltage. A unique aspect of this system is it can do all of this without human intervention. It constantly monitors the grid and can instantly react to situations of high or low voltage. We’re also continuing our investment and research activities around modern microgrid and battery energy storage technology. In 2025, we look forward to welcoming our member systems for education and training at our microgrid research center. This center will allow us to explore, alongside our members and education partners, the capabilities of modern microgrid technology. Greater grid resilience and energy demand support for our commercial customers are among the exciting opportunities we’re exploring. We’re also working to deploy our first grid-scale use of this technology to support greater grid resilience in a rural portion of the state. Additionally, we continue to partner with the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) on a wide range of research projects. These research activities will not only benefit our members but our industry. As part of our research partnership, we joined as founding members of two new EPRI initiatives in 2024 — DC Flex and GET SET. DC Flex (Data Center Flexibility) is an initiative looking at how the rapid growth of data centers, driven by advancements and adoption of AI, can serve as a way to support and stabilize the grid, while also improving efficiency and interconnection. The GET SET (Grid Enhancing Technologies for a Smart Energy Transition) initiative builds on EPRI’s more than a decade in progress grid enhancing technology research program to add a further focus on how these technologies can support the energy transition. When it comes to adding light to the stories of tomorrow, we think it will take a collaborative approach. And, we can’t wait to see where tomorrow takes us, together. More than Innovation The Middle Fork SVS makes sure that the voltage is not too low and it’s not too high. It injects reactive power (vars) to raise the voltage, or it can absorb reactive power from the transmission system in order to lower the voltage. A unique aspect of this system is the fact that it can do all of this without human intervention. 10 Back to Contents GRIDOVATION Investing Today
